title: Sorting and Slicing
objective: Sort an array with .sort(), reverse it with .reverse(), and pull out a sub-array with .slice().

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: array.sort() rearranges an array in place and, with no arguments, sorts it as strings — which works fine for words but silently gives the wrong order for numbers, since '10' sorts before '9' as text. To sort numbers correctly, pass a compare function: array.sort((a, b) => a - b) sorts ascending, and (b - a) sorts descending.
array.reverse() flips the current order of an array in place — first becomes last and last becomes first. It doesn't sort anything; it just reverses whatever order was already there.

array.slice(start, end) returns a brand-new array containing the elements from start up to, but not including, end — the original array is left completely unchanged. Leaving off end means 'to the end of the array'.
explanation.rule: sort() and reverse() both change the original array in place; slice() returns a new array and leaves the original untouched.

checks.question: const nums = [10, 2, 33]; nums.sort(); console.log(nums); — what prints, without a compare function?

feedback.correct: Correct — without a compare function, sort() compares elements as text, so '10' comes before '2' and '33', giving [10, 33, 2].
feedback.incorrect: Without a compare function, sort() treats numbers as text. Compare '10', '2', and '33' as strings character by character.

assignment.title: Leaderboard
assignment.brief: Write topTwo(scores) that returns a new array containing the two highest scores, sorted descending, without changing the original array's order.
requirements: Make a sorted copy (e.g. with slice()) so the original array isn't mutated.
Sort the copy descending using a compare function.
Return the first two elements of the sorted copy using slice().
assignment.outputCheckLabel: topTwo(scores) returns [90, 47] and leaves scores in its original order

hints: scores.slice() with no arguments makes a full copy, so sorting it won't touch the original scores array.
Sort the copy with (a, b) => b - a for descending order.
sorted.slice(0, 2) grabs the first two elements of the now-sorted copy.
The original scores array should still print in its original order afterward.
